title: Guru Angad's voice
hook: many saloks in the var are Guru Angad's, marked mahala 2

segments.voice: Yesterday, the pauri, and your line: step by step. We saw that some saloks beside the pauris aren't Guru Nanak's. Today, whose they are.

Open the Guru Granth Sahib and the Gurus' hymns are signed the same way: Nanak, in the closing lines, page after page. But Guru Nanak didn't write all of them. The later Gurus whose words are in the Granth also signed as Nanak. So how does a reader know who's speaking? A small label at the top of each composition: mahala, and a number. Mahala one, Guru Nanak. Mahala five, Guru Arjan. In the Asa di Var, every so often, the label reads mahala two. You've already heard that voice three times this block.
screen: `HYMN AFTER HYMN SIGNED: NANAK.` → `A LABEL AT THE TOP: MAHALA.` → `MAHALA TWO.`

segments.voice: Mahala two is Guru Angad, the second Guru. Before that he was Bhai Lehna, a devoted man from a village in Punjab who came to Guru Nanak at Kartarpur and stayed. Guru Nanak named him his successor and gave him a new name, Angad, which Sikhs often explain as ang, limb: a part of the Guru's own body. He left no long hymns in the Granth. What it holds of his is a set of saloks, many of them inside vars, beside Guru Nanak's pauris. Why sign as Nanak? Sikhs understand the Guruship as one light passing from body to body, the way one lamp lights another. Guru Angad isn't borrowing a name. In Sikh understanding it's the same light, speaking again; mahala two simply tells you which lamp. You've met that voice in this var. A hundred moons and a thousand suns, and still darkness without the Guru: mahala two, on day five hundred thirty-nine. Ego as a chronic illness with its medicine inside it: mahala two. The servant who argues: mahala two again. Listen across them and a voice emerges: short, practical, often about the Guru, about ego, about how a disciple actually behaves. It sounds like someone who spent years as a student before he became a teacher, and never forgot it. Sikh tradition remembers Guru Angad for teaching children, keeping the langar going, encouraging the Gurmukhi script and, some accounts say, for the wrestling ground. His saloks are the quiet second voice in the dawn song.
screen: `MAHALA TWO: GURU ANGAD.` · `ANG: A LIMB OF THE GURU.` · `ONE LIGHT, A SECOND LAMP.` · `SHORT, PRACTICAL, A STUDENT'S VOICE.` · then, large: `THE SECOND VOICE.`

segments.voice: If you have a gutka or an app, open the Asa di Var, look at the small headings, salok mahala one, salok mahala two, and read one marked two slowly. If you can't look it up, say one from this block once: the medicine is within. Notice how it sounds from a man who was first a student, and if you pray, say Waheguru.
Bhai Lehna, the name Guru Angad carried before he became Guru: his saloks, marked mahala two, are short, practical verses signed Nanak because, in Sikh understanding, it is one light.
Your line: the second voice. One light, a second lamp. That's day five hundred sixty-one.

howItsDone: Sikhs read the mahala heading above each composition in the Guru Granth Sahib to know which Guru wrote it, and Guru Angad's saloks are sung within Asa di Var and other vars.

chat.says: Every hymn in the Granth seems signed 'Nanak.' Did Guru Nanak write them all?
options: No: later Gurus signed Nanak too; the mahala label shows which, and mahala two is Guru Angad.
Yes: the other Gurus only collected and arranged them; Guru Nanak is the sole author.
No: 'Nanak' is just a word meaning hymn, added to the end of every verse in the book.
chat.meaning: The later Gurus also signed as Nanak, in Sikh understanding one light; the mahala number at the top shows which Guru, and two is Guru Angad.
